concept: Airdrops, points farming and spam airdrop token safety on Solana
summary: Airdrops are token distributions to wallets, often earned through off-chain points programs and filtered for sybils, and on Solana the same mechanism is abused by spam and scam tokens that lead to wallet drainers, cleaned up by hiding, burning, closing token accounts and revoking delegates. This pack catalogues 496 cited research units (503 scanned, 7 folded as duplicates) from 190 source URLs across program design, sybil filtering, farming economics, tax treatment, drainer mechanics, Token-2022 and cleanup safety. Evidence status: research claims ungated (v4 evidence gate not passed); treat as leads with cited sources.

facts.text: Burn is the step that makes a spam account closable. In Token-2022's process_burn the burned amount is subtracted from both the token account balance and the mint supply, and the account owner can authorize it unless the mint adds a restriction. The spl-token CLI's burn command accepts the keyword ALL as the amount. Sol Incinerator describes a burn as permanent: the tokens are gone and the supply stays lower.

Jito's December 2023 airdrop is the Solana case where a tiny stake paid very well. Jito sent 80M JTO to 9,852 addresses after sybil screening, about 8,100 JTO per address (derived). The lowest-points tier received 4,941 JTO each, roughly $14,000 at the $2.9 price Decentralised.co quoted on 2023-12-16 (derived). DL News (2023-12-07) said lowest-tier users could have staked one SOL, that the top tier received about 100,000 tokens, and that a mid-tier user got only 2.5 times the lowest tier. Filter aggressiveness is an explicit precision/recall dial. Wormhole says its filter strength is tunable along a spectrum. zkSync reportedly chose not to apply strict anti-sybil filtering, citing that 'Sybil detection often cuts out real users with arbitrary filters', and was then criticised (for example by Polygon's security chief) for leaving the airdrop highly farmable. A sybil tracker estimated about 135 million ZK might reach sybil wallets (preliminary).

Allium Labs is the analytics vendor behind several Solana airdrop filters. Wormhole says it ran ownership clustering, sybil detection and the rewards algorithm 'in partnership with' Allium. The Drift Foundation says it partnered with Allium to find sybil clusters. Sanctum says it flagged and blacklisted 61,181 wallets 'with Allium Labs'. The Drift post is Drift's own text: Allium republished it and notes it was 'originally written by drift'. The three posts give no sybil thresholds or code. The only airdrop the IRS names is one tied to a hard fork. Its Digital assets page, reviewed 2026-09-02, lists 'an airdrop as it relates to a hard fork' and 'a reward or award' as receipts that require a Yes answer to the Form 1040 digital asset question. In December 2019 an IRS special counsel said the IRS had no position on promotional airdrops, and TokenTax's farming guide, updated 2026-11-05, says no IRS guidance covers airdrop farming. Promotional, points-based and spam airdrops are therefore taxed by extrapolation from Rev. Rul. 2019-24.

A clean wallet preview is not proof that an approval or authority change is absent. In the Bull Checker case reported in 2024 (Jupiter and Offside Labs), a malicious Chrome extension replaced the wallet adapter's signTransaction, so the simulation looked normal while the signed transaction moved a victim's token authority to an attacker address. Scam Sniffer separately reports Solana drainers that use anti-simulation and fake simulation results. Blowfish released SafeGuard against simulation spoofing.

A balance-change preview is not proof of safety. Documented ways around it: an assign transaction that changes ownership without moving any balance (SlowMist, December 2025); programs that look clean at signing and flip state afterwards (Blowfish and Blockaid, 2024); anti-simulation tricks and fake simulation results, with victims confirming after a 'simulation failed' message (Scam Sniffer, January 2024); and Blockaid's January 2024 report that drainers 'can deceive the simulations used by Solana wallets'.

Cluster filters first remove entities that are not individual users. Arbitrum removes bridges, exchanges, smart contracts and CEX deposit addresses using Nansen, Hop and OffChain Labs data, plus manual removals such as donation addresses. Wormhole manually labelled contracts, relayer hot wallets and very large sybil clusters. Kaczyński and Wiącek advise excluding DEX and CEX addresses and not flagging an account merely for calling a high-degree contract such as a swap.

Cluster filters first remove entities that are not individual users. Arbitrum removes bridges, exchanges, smart contracts and CEX deposit addresses using Nansen, Hop and OffChain Labs data, plus manual cases such as donation addresses and L2 aliases. Wormhole manually labelled contracts, protocol relayer hot wallets and large sybil clusters of hundreds to thousands of wallets. Arbitrum's README lists Hop's blacklist and Hop's eliminatedSybilAttackers list among its inputs and gives no threshold for 'addresses with similar activity'.

Disclosing the reward pool and timeframe up front is the recommended points practice. Rooter, founder of Solend (a commercial interest), cites Solend Points Season 1: it published a minimum rewards pool that could only be increased (100,000 SLND at the start, later 100,000 PYTH and 10 Tensorians added) and a timeframe. Galaxy likewise says clearer disclosure of how points will be used would improve the practice and reduce regulatory exposure.

A clean wallet preview is not proof that a transaction is safe. ScamSniffer reports drainers using 'anti-simulation and fake simulation results'. GoPlus calls simulation 'not foolproof'. Phantom built Lighthouse-based Guard Instructions against simulation spoofing. Jupiter documented a live case.

Filter strictness is an explicit tuning choice. Wormhole says its sybil techniques 'lie on a spectrum via parameters that tune the aggressiveness of the filtering'. ZKsync says its sybil step 'intentionally used a very conservative heuristics framework, to avoid accidentally punishing real people'. Kaczyński and Wiącek make the score threshold a free parameter and warn that marking too many addresses as sybil may discourage honest users.

On Solana the key linking signal is the 'first funder': Allium defines it as the wallet that sends the initial SOL to a fresh wallet. Allium says farms that rotate several first-funder wallets can still be linked by tracing the original source of funds. It says its Solana sybil work with Wormhole, Jito and Jupiter produced a list of thousands of addresses in large sybil clusters, which Drift used as one input and which earned those wallets extra scrutiny. Wormhole separately says Allium helped build its source-of-funds and ownership-clustering analysis.

Exchange hot wallets are a false-positive source for cluster filters. Liu and Zhu note that many accounts receive funds from CEX hot wallets, forming perfect star patterns, and that accounts with few interaction types can look alike, so ordinary accounts 'might be tagged as Sybil's account by mistake'; they suggest multi-source interactions to reduce this. In a small HackMD funding-graph study (307 Mantle and 401 BSC wallets), 13 of 16 BSC hubs and 3 of 10 Mantle hubs were exchange wallets, and removing them cut members of clusters of 10 or more from 218 to 56 on BSC and from 217 to 142 on Man

In June 2026 the House Ways and Means Committee scheduled a 2026-06-09 hearing on six digital-asset tax bills and one discussion draft, which the Joint Committee on Taxation describes in JCX-18-26. The staking and mining bill, H.R. 9175 (introduced 2026-06-08), keeps current inclusion of newly minted validation rewards as ordinary income and adds an election to exclude them until disposition. EY says early drafts would defer staking rewards until disposal. A text search of the JCT document finds no use of the word 'airdrop', so none of these proposals addresses airdrops on its face.

Poisoning is a named way to create false positives. Kaczyński and Wiącek warn that a hunter can send tiny-value transfers to unrelated accounts to distort their topology, so a topology-only detector may mark honest users as sybils. Trusta reports that after Hop and Optimism opened community reporting, reported sybil accounts 'threatened to poison other wallets'. Neither source quantifies real incidents.

A delegate's reach is one token account and one amount. It does not extend to the wallet's other token accounts. MadeOnSol adds that it gives no control of native SOL in the wallet, although it does cover wrapped SOL held in the delegated token account.

Sybil detection is an arms race. Artemis says that once a model spots one type of fraud, fraudsters move to the next scheme. Messias et al. call defence against adaptive users 'an ongoing arms race'. Rickard predicted sybils would become nearly indistinguishable from real users. Kaczyński and Wiącek hypothesise that each detected topology pushes hunters toward noisier graphs until topology-only detection stops working.

Jupiter's own net-zero proposal describes the planned Jupuary 2026 (Option 1) as a 200M JUP initial distribution, a 200M bonus pool and 300M for Jupnet incentives (700M in total), with the eligibility checker due about a week after the vote and distribution about two weeks after that. A KuCoin News flash (from Odaily, 20 November 2025) reported the same structure at one-tenth scale: an initial airdrop to stakers and users who had paid transaction fees, a staking reward pool for users who keep airdropped tokens staked 'before the 2027 event', and a snapshot on 30 January 2026.

Funding-source and graph-clustering heuristics are the common core of airdrop sybil detection: Arbitrum's open-source pipeline builds transfer and funder/sweep graphs and splits large components with Louvain community detection, Wormhole uses source-of-funds analysis (direct and sequential 'diffusion funding') plus Louvain on transaction similarity, and Drift/Allium traces each wallet's first funder.

Airdrop sybil filters in the sources combine four signal types. (1) Funding: Wormhole traces 'diffusion' (wallet A funds B to Z) and 'sequential diffusion' (A funds B, B funds C) funding, Drift traces each wallet's first funder, and ZKsync groups wallets that share an ultimate funder or send to one CEX deposit address within a year. (2) Transfer graphs: Arbitrum builds a value-transfer graph and a funder/sweep graph, then splits large components with Louvain community detection. (3) Behaviour and timing: Wormhole runs Louvain on a transaction-similarity matrix built from timing, cadence and ac

SolPhishHunter's rules give a checklist for a suspicious transaction. STMT: more than 2 transfer instructions and at least 2 token balances going from non-zero to zero. AAT: any Assign instruction, or SetAuthority with authority type 'account owner'. ISA: a transfer that zeroes a balance toward an address matching 'Compu.*' or '.*1111'. Prerequisite filters skip market addresses and transactions whose logs contain buy, sell or purchase.

In the Token-2022 program source (main branch, fetched 2026-11-06) the transfer-hook CPI (Execute) runs only at the end of the transfer path; the burn and close handlers contain no hook call. Token-2022's docs likewise describe the hook as called during transfer. So burning a hook-bearing token and closing its account do not run the issuer's hook program, while any transfer of the token does.

Phantom combines third-party verification, machine-learning models, SimpleHash spam scores and user reports to auto-hide spam NFTs and every fungible token whose name contains a URL. It keeps an open-source community blocklist of malicious domains and contract addresses, shows Blowfish-powered Transaction Previews, and warns on address poisoning and copycat tokens. Phantom says it incubated Blowfish, so Phantom and Blowfish statements are not independent. Raydium notes that most Solana wallets ship a setting to hide spam or unknown tokens.

Liu and Zhu's Hop method builds a transaction graph per chain, measures the Jaccard similarity of each account's sequence of activity types, clusters similar sequences with DBSCAN, then inspects the clusters' transaction subgraphs for radial and sequential token-transfer patterns. The authors say the method needs the airdrop's eligibility prerequisites defined beforehand. Hop's own first pass removed small isolated connected components on the transaction graph.

Token creation on Solana is permissionless, and a token's name, ticker and logo are free text. Only the mint address identifies a token. Scammers copy real names and symbols with a different mint, and they put URLs or 'claim' instructions in token names and metadata. Phantom automatically hides every fungible token whose name contains a URL.

Most airdrop sybil filters cluster wallets by how money moved between them. Arbitrum builds graphs from value transfers and from 'funder' (first ether in) and 'sweep' (last ether out) transfers, then splits large components with Louvain community detection. Wormhole traces the source of funds ('diffusion' and 'sequential diffusion' funding) and runs Louvain on a transaction-similarity matrix. ZKsync groups externally owned accounts (EOAs) that share an ultimate funder or a CEX deposit address. For Drift, Allium traced each Solana wallet's first funder. Averages quoted for airdrop hunters describe repeat winners. X-explore and Colin Wu (2023-06-26) studied five large Ethereum airdrops (Uniswap, ENS, Optimism, Blur, Arbitrum). The 34,547 standard hunter addresses, which took part in three of the five, averaged $9,384 with a median of $6,497. The 932 premium addresses, which took part in all five and received tokens, averaged $18,935 with a median of $14,288. Both groups are selected for having won repeatedly, and ForkLog's summary gives no method detail.

Projects report excluding a large share of the wallets they checked, always on their own definition of sybil. Where a denominator is published: Sanctum's founder said 61,181 of 314,367 Wonderland registrants (about 20%) were marked and blacklisted after 'anti-sybil investigations' (the report gives no method). Hop's team identified 10,253 of 43,058 initially eligible addresses (about 24%) by removing small isolated connected components. Linea and Nansen flagged about 516,960 of 1,297,203 eligible addresses (about 40%), leaving 780,243. LayerZero cut an initial set of over two million potential

LayerZero's process shows how a crowd layer can swamp a filter. It cut an initial flag set of over two million addresses to a public list of 803,093 'to minimize false identifications', and said the list was not definitive until a final report. Its bounty stage opened on 18 May 2024 and required reports of at least 20 addresses with a clear methodology; the reward was 10% of the sybil's allocation. Geographic exclusions announced only at airdrop time drew backlash. EigenLayer let anyone deposit and earn points, then barred users from more than a dozen countries (including the U.S., Canada and China) from the airdrop; one investor said cutting the U.S. from an airdrop is fine, 'but then don't let them use it in the first place'. Galaxy notes Marginfi instead barred U.S.-based IP addresses from taking part in its points program, amid unclear U.S. regulation of points.

On Solana the fee component of cost is small: the base fee is a flat 5,000 lamports (0.000005 SOL) per signature, and priority fees are optional, with half burned and half kept by the leader. Fees are therefore not the main cost of a Solana farm; capital, time and wallet count dominate. The Helius page is undated, so the fee level should be re-checked against the Solana docs.

In the SolPhish data the three Solana-specific transaction types peaked in sequence. Impersonation of System Accounts (vanity addresses starting 'Compu' or ending in a run of '1', exploiting wallets that show only part of an address) came first and faded after June 2024; multi-transfer drains followed in March-April 2024 alongside the arrival of Solana drainer kits; Account Authority Transfer appeared later, which the authors attribute to phishers adapting to better wallet defences. That ordering is the authors' inference from one dataset.

Recourse exists at the large drops, but outcome data are rare. Linea published a webpage to check sybil status and let flagged users appeal. Wormhole took reconsideration requests through a form. Jupiter gave 3 months to appeal and earmarked part of its Carrots pool for appeals. LayerZero reported about 30,000 appeals. Of these four, only Linea published a reversal count (3.5k). A Jupiter forum thread from June 2025 holds forum assumptions about appeal sizes and no counts, and its posters treat the sybil review as not yet final. Those are forum posts, not Jupiter statements.

On Solana the fee part of a farm's cost is tiny. The base fee is 5,000 lamports (0.000005 SOL) per signature and is charged even when the transaction fails. The optional priority fee is compute units times the compute-unit price in micro-lamports. One thousand single-signature transactions therefore cost 0.005 SOL in base fees (derived). Capital, labour, wallet count and the chance of being filtered are the larger cost terms (inference from these figures). The subgraph-LightGBM paper (arXiv 2505.09313v1) reports precision 0.9428, recall 0.9182, F1 0.9303 and AUC 0.9806 on one data set: 193,701 addresses, 23,240 of them labelled sybil, from Binance's Account Bound (BAB) airdrop on BNB Smart Chain (January 2023 to May 2024), using 75 features from a two-layer transaction subgraph. On that data set it beats a clustering baseline attributed to Trusta (precision 0.7962, recall 0.8159). The authors say the model relies on data-set-specific features, so these figures are not evidence of performance on Solana.

Investors usually report non-business airdrop income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040). TaxAudit names Part I, line v, 'Digital assets received as ordinary income not reported elsewhere', and CoinLedger says Schedule 1 'Other Income' with a description such as 'crypto airdrop'. The IRS digital-assets page says to report income from forks, staking and mining on Schedule 1, and payments received as an independent contractor on Schedule C.

Kaczyński and Wiącek (International Journal of Electronics and Telecommunications, 2026) score ZKsync EOAs with four weighted steps: a graph isomorphism network (GIN) on funding-transfer topologies (star, chain, hybrid), DBSCAN on event-sequence similarity, DBSCAN on account-creation times within a 4-hour window, and a low-gas-usage test. At a 0.6 score threshold they flag 37,563 of 49,249 EOAs (about 76%). Of the 26,493 addresses flagged by the gas step, 24,651 had made no transaction, mostly 'dead' accounts created by hub wallets. IRS airdrop authority is limited to hard forks. Rev. Rul. 2019-24 holds only for 'an airdrop of a new cryptocurrency following a hard fork'. IRS FAQs 22-25 (Part I, transactions before 2025) and FAQs 104-107 (Part II, added 2025-12-15, last reviewed 2026-06-29) cover only hard-fork receipts, and the Part II page never uses the word airdrop. The IRS digital-assets page (reviewed 2026-09-02) lists 'an airdrop as it relates to a hard fork' among the receipts that make the Form 1040 digital-asset question a Yes.

Token-2022 extensions give scam tokens extra tricks beyond phishing links. PeckShield tied a burn scam (token 'RED', reported 2024-09-04) to the Permanent Delegate extension, which lets a mint's delegate burn tokens from any holder account (tokens burned seven seconds after purchase). Raydium's guidance says a malicious token program can charge fees on later interaction, a freeze authority or very high fee can trap buyers, and Token-2022 transfer hooks can run arbitrary code when a token account is closed.

A Token-2022 mint with the Permanent Delegate extension gives its delegate unlimited delegate privileges over every token account of that mint, so the delegate can burn or transfer any holder's balance, and can do so even when CPI Guard is on. The privilege is scoped to that mint's accounts. In September 2024 a buyer of a token called RED had the balance burned about seven seconds after the swap, and Jupiter and RugCheck then added indicators for the extension. For a spam token it means the issuer, not the holder, ultimately controls what sits in the account.

Rewarding raw activity counts attracts farmers. In Optimism's Airdrop 5 the 'Frequent User' bonus (10 or more app transactions a week in at least 20 weeks) cut 30-day retention by 7.1 percentage points, while 'Superchain Explorer' (activity on 7 or more chains) raised it 4.7 points and 'SuperFest Participant' raised it 10.0 points; the authors suspect farmers sell and leave. An academic study of nine airdrops makes the same point: when transaction count is the metric, low fees let farmers hit thresholds cheaply.

Do not swap, sell, bridge, claim, or send back an unsolicited token, and do not open the URL in its metadata even out of curiosity. Raydium says returning a token to the sender can trigger a malicious instruction; Data Clinic lists swap, sell, bridge and claim as actions to avoid.

The default for an unrecognized token is to hide or report it and do nothing else: do not click it, open its website or metadata links, swap, sell, bridge, claim or send it back. Phantom's Report as Spam hides the asset and feeds its spam detection (native tokens such as SOL have no such option). Data Clinic gives hide steps for Phantom, Ledger Live and Solflare-style wallets. Raydium says to turn on any 'hide spam/unknown tokens' wallet setting and not to send tokens back, because interaction may trigger a malicious instruction. The standard fake-airdrop drain has three steps. A lure sends the victim to a drainer site: a link in spam token or NFT metadata, a hijacked social account, an ad, a DM, or a fake 'claim' page. The site asks the victim to connect a wallet. It then asks for a signature on a transaction that moves assets to the attacker. Mandiant's CLINKSINK pages (fake airdrops themed on Phantom, DappRadar and BONK), ScamSniffer's NFT lures, and the Raydium, Phantom and Solflare guidance all describe this flow.

Address poisoning plants a lookalike address in a victim's history so the victim copies it later. Blockaid found a Telegram bot (reported March 2026) that automates this on Solana: it picks targets from top holders on DexScreener or Pump.fun, researches wallets on Solscan, generates a vanity address at a chosen similarity level, sends one-click dust, and forwards payouts. The bot claimed about $15,000 in SOL. Phantom warns when a user copies an address from history that they have not sent to before. Merely receiving an unsolicited token does not compromise a wallet and creates no ongoing charge. Phantom says an unfamiliar asset 'doesn't mean your wallet is compromised'. Data Clinic says no one can spend your SOL or other assets because a spam token arrived. Raydium places the danger in interacting with the token: visiting its metadata URL, connecting a wallet, or signing a fake claim. The SOL held in the account is a refundable deposit, not a fee (Raydium).

Closing an empty token account can break a program that pays into or trades through it. Marinade's help center (2026-10-07) says recipe rewards are airdropped to a payout token account in the wallet, that closing it stops the rewards, and that wallet features which sweep or close empty or low-balance token accounts can cause this; it advises excluding the payout token from any auto-close feature. Sol Incinerator likewise says to leave open an empty account that a trading bot (Autocompounder) still uses. Keep accounts you expect to receive into, and bulk-close only after checking.

On Solana the sender can create the recipient's associated token account (ATA) and pay for it. The ATA program's Create and CreateIdempotent instructions take a writable, signing 'funding account' and only a read-only, non-signing 'wallet address' for the new account. The SPL docs say the program exists so a token send works even when the receiver has no token account, and they name airdrop campaigns as the motive. So anyone can place an arbitrary mint in any wallet without a signature from its owner. This is how unsolicited tokens appear.

If a spam token was already interacted with, revoke any accidental approvals through a trusted site or the wallet's approval manager and check the token on Solscan without connecting the wallet. Data Clinic also describes unsolicited drops as a dusting privacy attack meant to track wallet activity, and advises keeping a record because disposal may be taxable under UK rules (tax treatment is a sibling concept).

Funding from centralized exchanges (CEXs) is the main evasion of funder tracing, and defenders answer with behaviour. Allium and Wormhole both say sophisticated farmers fund wallets directly from CEXs; Allium notes CEXs use the same wallets to process withdrawals for many users, which makes clusters harder to identify. Allium's answer is timing and behaviour clustering (for example a surge of wallets funded from one CEX address that made their first Drift deposits in a narrow window). A non-native SPL or Token-2022 token account can be closed only when its balance is zero, and this includes withheld transfer fees. So a spam balance must be burned (or moved) before the account can be closed. For Token-2022 accounts with withheld fees, anyone can call the permissionless harvest_withheld_tokens_to_mint instruction first, and the CLI close command does this harvest.

Spam NFTs carry the phishing site in the NFT's Name and External Link. In ScamSniffer's January 2024 Rainbow Drainer case, attackers airdropped such NFTs to holders of the ZERO token. Victims opened the site and signed even after the wallet reported that simulation failed, because the real transaction details were hidden. Phantom and Solflare both tell users never to click links inside unsolicited NFTs or tokens.

A farmer profits from a qualifying account only while its reward exceeds its cost. TierDrop (Yaish and Livshits, arXiv, 2024-07-01) models a farmer's utility per sybil account as the reward minus the eligibility cost scaled by a discount factor between 0 and 1, because farmers qualify more cheaply than ordinary users. Practitioner Kerman Kohli (2023-10-19) states the same rule in plain terms: as long as the cost to game an airdrop is less than the reward potential, airdrop farming will be prevalent.

Some dust in the activity feed is bait for a different attack, address poisoning, which burning or closing a token account does not address. A look-alike address sends a tiny transfer so that it sits near a real payment in history. Bitquery's study, reported by CryptoSlate on 2026-10-12, counted 4,497,798 Solana wallets targeted between 2025-10-30 and 2026-10-07 and found 1,104 qualifying payments worth $940,106 in a subset of about 3.0 million wallets poisoned through 2026-07-09; the article calls the loss figure a floor and says targeting is not loss. Receiving the dust does not itself drain

A frozen token account holding a balance may need thawing before it can be burned and closed, and only the freeze authority can thaw it. A mint creator can also use DefaultAccountState so that new token accounts start frozen. A spam token with an active freeze authority can therefore become permanently unburnable from the holder's side.

Operators instrument and screen victims. Scam Sniffer found Rainbow Drainer ran a self-hosted Matomo instance and tracked each step of the victim flow to improve conversion. Mandiant's CLINKSINK server returned 'null' when the same wallet connected twice, and its decrypted configuration held min_value_assets and min_value_connect thresholds (both 10, units not stated) and wording telling wallets that could not pay fees they were 'not eligible'.

Slorg, a member of Jupiter's Core Working Group, gave two reasons scammers burn buyers' tokens: to cause chaos, and to cut the circulating float so the price does not fall. PeckShield said burning manipulates circulating supply and tokenomics. Beosin said it could raise a token's price to profit through a related DeFi protocol. These are motives offered by commentators, not proven attributions.

Jupiter's claim flow required a 'Jupiverse Profile' (an email address plus connected wallets), but allocations stayed per wallet and linking wallets did not combine scores. SolanaFloor reported social-media frustration at the email-linking step. A January 2026 community post argued that per-wallet minimums penalise users who split stake across wallets.

Attackers reused one phishing NFT for a second campaign (MEMEDROP) by editing its name and link, with no new deployment. ScamSniffer suggested this worked because Solana had no blacklist for displaying such NFTs at the time. Phantom now hides reported spam NFTs and keeps a community blocklist, so this is a January 2024 observation.

Unsolicited tokens appear because anyone can create a token account for any wallet. The Associated Token Account program's Create and CreateIdempotent instructions need only the funding account to sign; the wallet that will own the new account is passed as a read-only, non-signer account. Circle's guide shows the same split (the payer signs and pays rent; the owner is just an address), and Phantom says anyone can send tokens or collectibles to a wallet without its permission. The sender funds the account's rent; the recipient signs nothing.

Phantom announced a Burn Token tab for spam NFTs in August 2022 (Cointelegraph, 2022-08-18) and promised more automated spam detection. Phantom's current help pages on unfamiliar tokens and token security signals describe hiding and reporting but do not mention burning, and Phantom's original 2022 blog post returned HTTP 404 when fetched on 2026-11-06 (a search result still lists it). Whether a wallet-native burn or close is still offered for tokens in Phantom, Solflare or Backpack is unconfirmed.

Reward design decides whether extra wallets pay. TierDrop proves that when each eligible account gets a fixed reward and farmers can create unlimited sybil accounts, the issuer faces unbounded losses unless the farmers' cost to qualify exceeds the issuer's cost per account or every sybil is detected (Theorem 7.1). When a fixed pool is split equally among eligible accounts, farmers add accounts only until the share per account equals their cost, so total farmer profit is bounded and each extra wallet earns less (Claim 7.3). TierDrop (arXiv, July 2024; authors at Matter Labs, an L2 developer) models two payout designs. Fixed reward per eligible account: if farmers can create unlimited sybil accounts, the issuer faces unbounded losses unless its cost to issue one reward is no higher than the farmer's cost to qualify (Theorem 7.1). Pro-rata pool (a fixed token budget split among all eligible accounts): farmers stop adding accounts when the reward per account falls to their cost, so the equilibrium number of farmer accounts is the pool divided by (lambda times cost), minus the honest eligible accounts (Claim 7.3). Projects use earlier airdrops' sybil flags in different ways. Arbitrum's listed inputs include Hop's blacklist and its eliminatedSybilAttackers list. Allium treated a flag from another airdrop as a higher propensity that earned extra scrutiny for Drift, not as proof. Since 2025-01-01 a US taxpayer must track digital-asset basis wallet by wallet or account by account, not as one universal pool. Rev. Proc. 2024-28 let taxpayers make a one-time reasonable allocation of unused basis to each wallet or account as of that date. For an airdrop farmer, income from every wallet combines on one return because there is one taxpayer, but basis follows each wallet. Without specific identification, brokers must apply FIFO within each account, and self-custody holders may adopt a standing identification rule in their records.

Receiving an unsolicited Solana token or NFT does not itself compromise a wallet; the harm starts when the holder visits the claim URL in its name or metadata, connects a wallet, or signs a transaction. Wallet and DEX safety guides agree on this and tell users not to click, visit, sell, or 'send back' such assets.

Timing rules for push, claim-based and locked airdrops are interpretations of dominion and control, not IRS rules. TokenTax says a push airdrop is taxable when usable tokens arrive, a claim-based airdrop when the claim gives control, and a locked token when the lock ends; unclaimed allocations are generally not taxed. CoinLedger says the IRS has not said whether income arises when an airdrop becomes available or when it is claimed, and expects a dominion-and-control test.

Opaque or shifting conversion rules trigger backlash. EigenLayer's May 2024 airdrop drew criticism for non-transferable tokens, exclusion of users in more than a dozen countries who could still deposit, and unclear treatment of points earned through liquid restaking. Tensor and EigenLayer both revised terms after criticism, and Blur was criticised for extending its points window and changing airdrop rules. Compound's founder called points the largest information asymmetry in crypto.

Geographic limits applied after points accrue repeatedly cause anger. Marginfi barred U.S. IP addresses from its points program from the start. Galaxy ties this to legal uncertainty over whether points redeemable for tokens invite securities scrutiny (analysis dated 22 July 2024; the legal position may have changed since).

This matters for airdrop farmers using many wallets, because the income from all wallets is combined on one return but basis follows each wallet.

Standard practitioner method: the fair market value included as income when the airdrop is received becomes the cost basis, so a later sale is taxed only on the change from that value. The one open-source accounting tool skimmed (Onchain-Accounting) documents the same rule. Record the USD price at the moment of claim or receipt.

Timing for claim-based and locked airdrops is a vendor interpretation of dominion and control, not IRS guidance. TokenTax says push airdrops are taxable when usable tokens arrive, claim-based airdrops when the claim gives control, and locked tokens after the lockup ends. Unclaimed airdrops are generally not taxed until control exists.

The Token-2022 source requires the current permanent delegate to sign SetAuthority(PermanentDelegate). The Solana docs page says the mint authority can rotate the permanent delegate. The two statements agree only when the same address holds both roles. Treat the code as the rule.

A delegate can transfer or burn tokens from the approved token account, up to the delegated amount. Each delegate transfer or burn lowers the delegated amount, and both token programs clear the delegate field when it reaches zero. A small allowance therefore ends through use. A large allowance stays active until the owner revokes it.

Rev. Rul. 2023-14 (IRB 2023-33) applies the same dominion-and-control timing test to staking rewards: the fair market value, measured when the taxpayer gains dominion and control, is gross income for that year. The ruling does not mention airdrops. Its footnote 3 says it does not address other rules such as IRC section 83.

In Paschall v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-46, the Tax Court held that Cardano staking rewards credited by eToro were gross income in the year credited, because the taxpayer had dominion and control. The court rejected the self-created-property theory and the stock-dividend analogy. It rested on IRC section 61 and case law and did not rely on Rev. Rul. 2023-14. EY notes limited precedential value: a memorandum opinion, a stipulated record and a pro se taxpayer. The IRS lists the decision on its Digital assets page. It concerns staking and does not discuss airdrops.

For a hard-fork airdrop the IRS FAQ (A24, A25) says income equals the fair market value when received, which is when the transaction is recorded on the distributed ledger, provided the holder has dominion and control. Basis equals the amount included in income. For crypto received outside an exchange, FAQ A27 sets the value at the date and time recorded on the ledger and accepts a blockchain explorer's value as evidence. A later sale is reported on Form 8949, and ordinary income from forks, staking and mining goes on Schedule 1.

In Paschall v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-46, the Tax Court held that Cardano staking rewards credited to a taxpayer's eToro account in 2021 were gross income when credited, not when sold. It found dominion and control from the ability to sell despite temporary limits on external transfers, and rejected the stock-dividend (Eisner v. Macomber) and self-created-property analogies. The IRS lists the memo as 'Cryptocurrency staking rewards are income'. EY's account of the opinion does not mention airdrops.

The allowance is stored apart from the token balance, and a transfer signed by the owner leaves the delegate fields unchanged. Emptying a token account therefore does not revoke its delegate, and a delegate approved for more than the balance can also spend tokens that arrive later. A delegate ends when its allowance is used up, when the owner sends Revoke, when a new Approve replaces it, when SetAuthority changes the account owner, or when the account is closed. This is a reading of both programs' source, not a documented guarantee.

They suggest a lower score for 1-hop neighbours of flagged hubs but kept the full score of 1. Rev. Rul. 2019-24 holds that a taxpayer has ordinary gross income under IRC section 61 when they receive units of new cryptocurrency from an airdrop following a hard fork. The amount is the fair market value when received. In the ruling's example the holder has dominion and control because they can immediately dispose of the units.

For UK airdrops not taxed as income, base cost is uncertain. Recap reports no HMRC guidance on acquisition cost and suggests nil cost when tokens are issued directly to the recipient. For income-taxed airdrops, receipt-date market value is the acquisition cost.

Rev. Rul. 2019-24 holds that a taxpayer has ordinary income under IRC section 61 when the taxpayer receives units of a new cryptocurrency in an airdrop that follows a hard fork. The amount is the fair market value when the airdrop is recorded on the distributed ledger, and that amount becomes the taxpayer's basis. A hard fork with no airdrop produces no income. The ruling's worked example finds dominion and control because the holder could dispose of the new units immediately.

The IRS ties receipt to dominion and control, not to the ledger entry alone. Rev. Rul. 2019-24 says a taxpayer has not received an airdropped coin if an exchange does not yet support it. The taxpayer is treated as receiving it when the ability to transfer, sell, exchange or otherwise dispose of it arrives. The same ruling warns that a taxpayer may constructively receive a coin before the airdrop is recorded. IRS FAQ A25 repeats the test: the taxpayer has received the coin when they can transfer, sell, exchange or otherwise dispose of it.

The IRS gives no valuation rule for an airdropped token that has no market. FAQ A27 accepts a blockchain explorer's value or requires the taxpayer to show the value used is accurate. FAQ A28 sets value at the fair market value of the property or services given, but it covers only crypto received in exchange for property or services. TokenTax says a token with no quoted price is not automatically worth zero, so keep screenshots, on-chain records and liquidity data. Koinly suggests using the value from when a market first becomes available.

If an airdrop pays for services performed as an independent contractor, the IRS treats its fair market value at receipt as self-employment income (FAQ A10). The IRS Digital assets page sends independent-contractor payments to Schedule C. This is the IRS rule for payment for services in virtual currency; the IRS has not said when a task-based airdrop counts as such payment.

The page does not state the allowable cost for an airdrop that was not charged to Income Tax. Recap, a UK tax-software vendor whose page shows it was last updated about four years ago, says there is no HMRC guidance on that cost and suggests nil when tokens are issued directly to the recipient. The amount is the fair market value when the airdrop is recorded on the ledger, provided the holder has dominion and control. In the ruling's example the holder can dispose of the units immediately. A hard fork that delivers no new units produces no income.

For airdrops outside hard forks, practitioners fill the gap with the breadth of section 61 and report ordinary income at fair market value when the holder gains control. TokenTax says to report promotional airdrops as ordinary income at receipt anyway. TaxAudit (2025-06-10) says airdropped crypto and NFTs are reportable 'until further guidance arrives'. CoinLedger (2026-01-02) says tax professionals generally treat airdrops as ordinary income at receipt. This is professional consensus, not IRS authority.

For UK Capital Gains Tax, HMRC's CRYPTO22350 says airdropped tokens go into their own section 104 pool unless the recipient already holds that token, and that section 43 TCGA 1992 does not apply because the value does not derive from tokens already held. Neither HMRC page states a base cost for an airdrop not taxed as income. Recap's guide (marked last updated about four years ago) calls that area uncertain, suggests nil cost for tokens issued directly to the recipient, and takes receipt-date market value as cost for income-taxed airdrops.

Treatment of a passive, unsolicited airdrop differs by jurisdiction as of November 2026. The US has authority only for hard-fork airdrops, where income arises at control, and practitioners extend that to other airdrops. The UK says Income Tax may not apply when nothing was done in return, leaving Capital Gains Tax on disposal. Australia's draft ruling would not tax a non-business recipient on receipt. In all three, an airdrop given for a service or task is income.

A delegate can transfer or burn. Each delegate Transfer or Burn reduces delegated_amount, and the program clears the delegate when the amount reaches 0. A small Approve therefore ends by use. An Approve sized to the whole balance stays live until the owner revokes it, replaces it or spends it.

CPI Guard does not stop an existing delegate or the permanent delegate from transferring or burning through CPI. It does not block Revoke. It does not stop a top-level Approve that the owner signs, because the Approve check applies only inside CPI. It narrows CPI-based approval grabs and nothing more.

The August 2022 Slope drain shows why revocation is irrelevant after a key compromise. Sentry says 9,231 wallets were drained from 22:37 UTC on 2 August 2022 with transactions signed by private keys. Ackee, in January 2023, counts 9,229 wallets and about 4.1 million dollars, agrees the transactions were signed correctly, and says the root cause was never conclusively explained.

Revoking moves, sells or burns nothing, because the instruction only clears the delegate fields, and it costs only the network fee. If the owner still uses the dApp that set the approval, Solana Compass says the dApp asks for a new approval next time.

Phantom's help centre article on revoking approvals (undated when fetched) points users to a third-party tool, Famous Foxes' Revoker. The steps are to connect Phantom and choose 'Revoke all'. It names no built-in delegate-revoke screen.

Disconnecting a dApp or wallet session does not remove an on-chain delegate. Phantom, the Solana Mobile wallet help and MadeOnSol each say the approval stays active after disconnecting. The Solana Mobile help adds that it ends only when the owner revokes it or the approved amount is spent.

A delegate's transfers decrement delegated_amount, and the delegate is cleared when the allowance reaches 0. A bounded Approve therefore expires by use; an Approve for a very large amount stays live until revoked.

To find delegates, call getTokenAccountsByOwner with jsonParsed encoding and a programId filter for each token program, then read delegate and delegatedAmount in each account's parsed info. getTokenAccountsByDelegate does the reverse and lists the token accounts whose delegate matches a given address. Solana Compass's scanner follows the first method and keeps only accounts with a non-zero approved amount.

Searchers needed at least 1 SOL of tips between epochs 366 and 536 and fell into five tiers.

Cleanup tools take a share of the recovered rent. A small HackMD funding-graph report on Mantle and BSC airdrop lists shows the common recipe. CLINKSINK flow per Mandiant: obfuscated JavaScript checks for Phantom, POSTs an affiliate ID, receives an AES-encrypted config (receiver wallet, revenue split, UI text), looks up the connected wallet's balance, then asks for a signature; typical split is 80% affiliate and 20% operator (operator share ranged 5-25%). If the victim rejects the transaction, the theft fails.

The payout is not knowable in advance. Points programmes carry no hard commitment: the project may or may not convert points into a token, can change criteria and conversion rates, and can invalidate points from addresses it judges to be multi-account farming. One farmer quoted by The Block estimated that only 10% to 15% of projects give airdrops, and The Block notes that a farmer may lose money if an airdrop never happens. Expected value therefore has to be weighted by the chance that a token is issued at all.

Published exclusion counts differ widely and use different denominators, so they are not comparable. Sanctum blacklisted 61,181 of 314,367 registered Wonderland wallets (19.5%) with Allium Labs (post of 2024-07-16). Linea and Nansen flagged about 516,960 of 1,297,203 eligible addresses (39.9%), leaving 780,243. Jupiter flagged 750,000+ wallets out of 'more than 10m' that used it, at most 7.5%. LayerZero's preliminary list had 803,093 addresses after a first pass of over two million. The percentages are my arithmetic on the issuers' own figures. No issuer's count has independent validation.

MEV searchers shared 5,000,000 JTO if they tipped at least 1 SOL in total between epochs 366 and 536, in five tiers. For both groups 50% was claimable at genesis and 50% vested linearly over 12 months.

Jito's ten point tiers were built so smaller holders receive more per point than under a linear model.

Payout is not knowable in advance. Cost-per-user figures understate what an airdrop costs the issuer, because few recipients stay. Kerman Kohli notes that the usual calculation (airdrop dollars divided by addresses claimed) ignores retention, and estimates that only 10% to 20% of addresses hold, so the true cost is 5 to 10 times higher (his estimate, not a dataset). Phishers use System Program Assign on a wallet account and SetAuthority on token accounts. Of 8,571 suspicious transactions flagged, 2,272 (26.51%) were authority transfers. Of those, 2,171 were confirmed phishing, all with a wallet-account transfer and 1,391 also with a token-account transfer.

The article does not analyse points programs as a factor.

Allocations are heavily skewed, so the mean overstates the typical recipient. For Hyperliquid (2024-11-29, more than 94,000 recipients), ASXN data cited by ForkLog gave a mean of 2,881.73 HYPE (about $100,000 on 2024-12-23) against a median award near $2,250, with 56.6% of recipients getting 100 tokens or fewer. TokenTax says farming classified as a business is reported on Schedule C and bears 15.3% self-employment tax, while hobby income goes on Schedule 1 line 8j with no expense deductions after 2025. The classification turns on the IRC section 183 nine-factor test. This is one vendor's reading; no IRS authority on farming was found.

TokenTax says airdrop farming that reaches the level of a trade or business is reported on Schedule C and bears 15.3% self-employment tax once net earnings reach $400. Hobby-level farming goes on Schedule 1 line 8j with no expense deductions after 2025, because the One Big Beautiful Bill Act made the elimination of miscellaneous itemized deductions permanent. The classification turns on the nine-factor test under IRC section 183. This is one vendor's reading; no IRS authority on farming was found.

Reported Solana drainer losses depend on tracker scope: Scam Sniffer (2024-01-13) put Rainbow plus Node Drainer at about $4.17M from about 3,947 victims in roughly a month; Mandiant extrapolated at least about $900k for CLINKSINK affiliates from the operator's 20% share. These are different drainer sets and methods, so they are not additive or comparable.

Solana drainers are sold as services. It derived this from at least 1,491 SOL plus tokens worth over $180,000 reaching one operator address, divided by the 20% share. Mandiant warns that address may also hold funds from the operator's own campaigns, so the figure is an estimate.

Widely repeated airdrop ROI statistics trace back to a vendor page and could not be verified. ChainScore Labs cites a Nansen analysis of 10 major L2 airdrops with a median net profit of $47 and a mean of $1,850, says more than 80% of recipients sell within a week, and says mainnet gas can exceed $500 per wallet. A targeted search found no Nansen publication, and the page's case-study table is illustrative. These figures are not used as evidence in this file.

Older Solana fee explainers are out of date on priority fees. Helius (early 2024) says the leader keeps 50% of a priority fee and the other 50% is burned. The SIMD-0096 feature gate moves 100% of the priority fee to the validator, and an Eco support article fetched 2026-10-13 states that priority fees are not burned while half of the base fee still is. The farmer pays the same amount either way, so a cost model that deducts a priority-fee burn is wrong.

The farmer's decision rule is that farming continues as long as the cost to game an airdrop is below the potential reward; a simple expected-value model compares money put in against money expected back. One advocate puts a mainnet swap at about $50 of gas and argues small accounts can multiply 10-100x, while admitting a stated conflict of interest (he farms Solana and Celestia himself).

Unsourced false-positive figures circulate. A ChainScore Labs blog page gives 5-15% 'legit users blocked' for naive heuristics and '>50%' false positives in an unattributed trend line, cites no study, data set or method, and is promotional. An earlier scout note attributing a '15-30%' rate to this page is not supported by the page text. Treat these numbers as unverified.

ARTEMIX tested single rules against its labels. A self-trading rule flagged 1,303 addresses, of which 694 (53%) carry hunter labels, and it covered only 14.4% of the 4,808 labelled hunters. Combining rules, community detection and boosting raised F1 to 0.898. The labels come from an earlier data set, so these shares measure agreement with that data set, not truth.

The risk starts when the holder interacts with the token. Do not click links attached to it, visit its website, open the URL in its metadata, claim, swap, sell, bridge, approve, or send it back. Raydium says the metadata often carries a URL such as 'Visit xyz-airdrop.com to claim!' that phishes a seed phrase, asks for a drain signature, or embeds a malicious token program, and adds 'Do not try to send them back. Mandiant saw CLINKSINK pages themed as PHNTM, DappRadar, Phantom and BONK airdrops that asked holders to connect a wallet and sign to claim; if the victim rejected the transaction, the theft failed. Scam Sniffer saw phishing NFTs airdropped to ZERO holders with the site in the Name and External Link fields, and victims who confirmed after a 'simulation failed' warning. Phantom shows a warning for any token with the extension. In the September 2024 'RED' case, a buyer's tokens were burned seven seconds after the swap with no further action by the holder; per Jupiter's Slorg, Jupiter and RugCheck added indicators for the extension. A mint that still has a freeze authority can freeze a holder's token account, which then cannot receive, transfer or burn until thawed (a frozen account can be closed only at zero balance); revoking the authority removes the ability. Jupiter's Shield API labels HAS_FREEZE_AUTHORITY a 'warning' and HAS_MINT_AUTHORITY 'info', and Raydium lists a freeze authority among the ways a fake token can trap buyers.

Receiving an airdrop does not create a delegate. Approve needs the token account owner's signature, and an airdrop sender cannot sign for the recipient. A standard delegate appears only if the owner signs an Approve or ApproveChecked, so the risk sits in unexpected signing prompts, such as fake airdrop claim sites, not in the receipt of spam tokens. The Token-2022 permanent delegate is the one case where such an authority exists without the holder's signature.

Accounts keep the lamports they were funded with, so a token account created before a rent step holds more than the new minimum. The owner can withdraw that excess with the WithdrawExcessLamports instruction without closing the account or touching its tokens; it works on Token and Token-2022 accounts, not wrapped SOL, and needs the owner's signature. Raydium says frozen token accounts remain eligible and the Token-2022 handler contains no frozen check, so excess can be reclaimed even from a spam account that cannot be burned or closed. Raydium advises that closing airdropped token accounts to reclaim rent is risky for Token-2022 tokens with transfer hooks, and recommends simply leaving spam tokens alone. This is a single-source warning; no source checked says whether burn or close instructions invoke a transfer hook.

A frozen token account that still holds tokens can be neither burned nor closed by its owner. Burn fails with AccountFrozen in both token programs, only the mint's freeze authority can thaw the account, and a Token-2022 mint can use DefaultAccountState so every new account starts frozen. An empty frozen account is different: neither program's CloseAccount handler checks the frozen flag, and Sol Incinerator says such an account 'can sometimes close without thawing'. Jupiter lists Has Freeze Authority as a Shield warning, and Streamflow's Dust Collector skips frozen accounts.

Error strings seen during cleanup and their causes: 'Non-native account can only be closed if its balance is zero' (NonNativeHasBalance: burn or move the tokens first); 'Account is frozen' (the freeze authority froze the account while it holds tokens); 'An account can only be closed if its withheld fee balance is zero, harvest fees to the mint and try again' (Token-2022 withheld fees); 'Instruction does not support native tokens' (WithdrawExcessLamports against a wrapped-SOL account). If a malicious signature has been given, Raydium advises moving any remaining funds to a new wallet immediately and states that Solana transactions are final, with funds sent to a scammer not recoverable absent law-enforcement action. After an owner-replacement drain, self-help can fail: in SlowMist's case the victim's attempts to transfer and to revoke from the compromised account all failed.

SPL Token and Token-2022 accounts support WithdrawExcessLamports, which moves lamports above the account's current rent-exempt minimum to a destination the authority chooses. It takes no amount, is idempotent, does not close the account, and leaves the token balance untouched; a frozen token account is still eligible. Wrapped SOL accounts are not supported (error 'Instruction does not support native tokens'); close those instead. For a spam account this is a third option beside leaving it alone or burning and closing: recover excess rent and keep the account open. An account created after step

With CPI Guard enabled on a Token-2022 token account, the program rejects these instructions when another program invokes them through CPI: owner-signed Transfer and Burn, Approve and ApproveChecked, CloseAccount to a non-owner destination, and SetAuthority that adds or replaces the close authority. Changing the token account owner with SetAuthority stays blocked even outside CPI (error CpiGuardOwnerChangeBlocked).

Published eligibility checkers act as the error-surfacing step. Jito's checker was live while claiming was not yet open (2023-12-04); Jupiter's checker and 'Jupiverse Profile' went live on 2025-01-15 about a week before launch, with three months to appeal an allocation. Aster (a BNB Chain perps exchange) delayed its airdrop to 2025-10-20 after the community flagged allocation inconsistencies, and gave users 48 hours after the update to choose a USDT refund instead.

The SPL Burn instruction subtracts the amount from both the token account's balance and the mint's total supply; it does not send tokens to a null address. It needs the owner's (or an approved delegate's) signature, fails on a frozen account (AccountFrozen) and on wrapped-SOL accounts (NativeNotSupported), and cannot be undone: Sol Incinerator and Streamflow both state that burning permanently destroys the tokens.

A Transfer Hook mint makes Token-2022 call a custom program on every transfer of that mint. The hook can refuse transfers (Solana's docs list wallet allow and deny lists as a use and show a sample hook that fails transfers above a size limit), so a creator can in principle use one to block transfers to chosen wallets, including sales. Token-2022 converts every account in the hook call to read-only, so the sender's signer privileges do not extend to the hook program, a choice the docs say prevents malicious use. Phantom supports hooks and describes them as deciding whether a transfer is allowed

A merkle airdrop leaf must hold the immutable snapshot amount. A CodeHawks contest finding (Snowman Merkle Airdrop, 12-19 June 2025, EVM) showed a claim function rebuilding the leaf from the receiver's live balance, so any transfer after the snapshot made the proof fail and locked out legitimate claimants; the fix passes the snapshot amount into both leaf and signature check.

Token-2022 adds close conditions beyond a zero balance. An account holding withheld transfer fees cannot close until they are harvested to the mint; the harvest_withheld_tokens_to_mint instruction is permissionless and the spl-token close command performs it. The close handler also requires any confidential-transfer state on the account to report itself closable. If CPI Guard is enabled and the close happens inside a CPI, the lamport destination must be the account owner. Token-2022 has two special cases for clearing unwanted accounts. Non-transferable (soul-bound) tokens cannot be sold or sent, but the docs say the owner can burn and close the account, so burning is how to clear them. An account holding withheld transfer fees cannot close until they are harvested: anyone can call the permissionless harvest_withheld_tokens_to_mint instruction, and the spl-token close command does it for you. process_close_account also runs closable() checks on transfer-fee and confidential-transfer state.

Token-2022's PermanentDelegate is a mint-level authority that can transfer or burn tokens in any token account of that mint, with no amount limit and no signature from the holder. Token account owners cannot revoke it, and Revoke clears only the per-account delegate field. It applies only to token accounts of the mint that carries it, so an airdropped spam mint with a permanent delegate exposes that spam balance, not the recipient's other tokens.

Jupuary 2025 (checker published 2025-01-15) split 700M JUP into Users 440M, Stakers 60M and 'Carrots' 200M. Users were Swap Users plus Expert Traders, who use Perps, limit orders, DCA and similar products; Expert Traders got 70M JUP across about 270k wallets, tiered on volume and individual trade size. About 2 million wallets were due tokens, against 955,000 in the first round, and Jupiter warned that many qualified wallets would get less than in 2024.

As published by Jupiter on 15 January 2025, Jupuary round 2 divided 700M JUP into 440M for users (Swap Users, plus 70M for about 270k 'Expert Traders' of Perps, limit orders, DCA, value averaging and Ape), about 60M for stakers, and 200M 'Carrots' held back and left out of the checker. About 2 million wallets qualified. A wallet that qualifies as both Swap User and Expert Trader receives both allocations.

Users reported eligibility-checker errors in two Jupiter cycles. On launch day of the Jupuary 2025 checker, one user with over $100k volume (about $180k on Dune) said they were placed in the wrong tier and that limit-order activity and cancellations were not counted, and another said the gap between the $10k and $100k swap tiers was too big. A January 2026 post alleged the checker returned '0', 'not eligible' or blank for the same wallet depending on the session. These are unverified user reports; no team reply appears on either page.

Signing through a warning is a repeat failure. Victims in ScamSniffer's ZERO case confirmed the transaction after a 'simulation failed' notice. Phantom says to stop and verify when its simulation raises a warning. Raydium says to reject any prompt that does not match the action the site claimed, for example 'transfer all your USDC' where a swap was expected.

A Token-2022 NonTransferable ('soul-bound') spam token cannot be sent anywhere, but its owner can still burn it and close the account. The docs say the extension 'allows the owner to burn and close the account if they want', and the program's burn handler contains no NonTransferable check.

A non-native token account closes only at a zero balance. The SPL Token interface error NonNativeHasBalance reads 'Non-native account can only be closed if its balance is zero', and Token-2022's process_close_account returns that same error when the account is not native and its amount is not zero. The dollar value a wallet shows is irrelevant: a dust balance or an unpriced token still counts as a balance and blocks the close. An unwanted balance must therefore be burned (or moved) before the account can be closed.

A holder cannot burn, and so cannot close, a spam balance when the issuer has frozen the account or paused the mint. process_burn returns AccountFrozen for a frozen account and MintPaused for a mint paused through the Pausable extension. Only the freeze authority can thaw an account, and the DefaultAccountState extension lets a creator start every new account frozen. A spam token with a live freeze authority can therefore leave a balance the holder cannot clear; hiding is the only holder-side step left. A durable-nonce transaction replaces the recent blockhash with a stored nonce, so it loses the roughly 150-slot expiry and stays valid until the nonce is advanced; Solana's docs describe this as enabling offline signing and delayed submission, and add a warning that durable nonces may be deprecated in a future release. The SolPhish paper found 14 multi-transfer phishing transactions that used the advanceNonce instruction and reads this as letting phishers hold a signed transaction for later execution, which delays the loss and lowers the chance of detection.

Authority flags also appear on legitimate, centrally issued tokens. Jupiter's Shield documentation example flags the USDC mint (EPjFWdd5AufqSSqeM2qN1xzybapC8G4wEGGkZwyTDt1v) with HAS_FREEZE_AUTHORITY and HAS_MINT_AUTHORITY, and a public-RPC read of that mint account on 2026-11-06 shows both authorities set. Raydium's rule of thumb that a fake USDC 'will have a live mint authority' therefore cannot separate the real mint from a fake; the canonical-mint-address check Raydium also gives can.

Jupiter's Shield endpoint returns per-mint warnings for freeze authority, mint authority, unverified status, low organic activity and new listings, says the list will change, and notes the Ultra Swap API is no longer actively maintained (superseded by Swap V2). Per one news report, OKX Wallet warned on 7 January 2026 about owner-permission phishing, said it had updated its detection and prompts, said Phantom has similar risk markings, and said many other mainstream wallets had not yet updated. This is a single secondary report of OKX's statement.

A preview that shows no balance change is not proof of safety. An owner reassignment shows no change (SlowMist, OKX). A time-of-check drain shows a benign result at simulation (Blockaid). Treat Assign, SetAuthority with authority type 'account owner', unknown programs, and nonce-advance instructions as high risk even when balances look unchanged.

Raydium says Solana transactions are final and that funds sent to a scammer cannot be recovered without law enforcement. If you signed a malicious transaction, it says to move remaining funds to a new wallet at once.

Token-2022 rejects SetAuthority account-owner changes on accounts with the ImmutableOwner extension (error ImmutableOwner), and the Associated Token Account program creates every associated token account with that extension when the token program is Token-2022. In the classic Token program, InitializeImmutableOwner is a no-op that only logs 'Please upgrade to SPL Token 2022 for immutable owner support', so an associated token account of a classic-token mint can still be reassigned with SetAuthority.

Phantom's help page says reporting an asset as spam hides it and feeds spam detection, and that native tokens such as SOL cannot be reported as spam. The page does not mention burning or selling and carries no date.

Treat the cleanup steps as a ladder of increasing permanence. Hiding is non-destructive: Phantom lets a user undo a mistaken spam hide with 'Report as not spam'. Burning is permanent. Closing an empty account only returns its deposit and can be undone by paying rent again to reopen the associated token account; Sol Incinerator says 'A close is easy to reverse' and 'A burn is permanent', and Streamflow says a closed account cannot be reversed but the rent can be paid again to reopen it.

Phantom hides tokens it believes are spam and shows 'This token was hidden because Phantom believes it is spam'; it says reporting an asset as spam hides it and helps improve spam detection, and a mistaken hide can be reversed with 'Report as not spam'. Native tokens such as SOL cannot be reported. Phantom's token security signals page defines Mintable, Freezable ('a significant red flag'), Mutable and LP Locked. Neither Phantom page mentions burning or closing token accounts.

An owner-change transaction shows no balance change in a wallet preview, so a wallet that only shows balance deltas can look safe. SlowMist said the attacker's transaction showed no fund changes, and that users used to Ethereum may not know a Solana account's owner can be changed. OKX Wallet's January 2026 warning makes the same point: the simulation shows 'No balance change'.

An Approve covers one token account and one amount, not the whole wallet. Solana's docs say the delegate cannot drain the account beyond the approved amount. MadeOnSol warns that a malicious flow can still request several approval instructions or signatures, so each request needs its own check.

Token-2022's Permanent Delegate is a mint extension giving a designated address unrestricted burn and transfer power over every token account of that mint. Revoke only clears the per-account delegate field, so the holder cannot remove it. In the Token-2022 code, only the current permanent delegate can change it via SetAuthority(PermanentDelegate). In September 2024 a token called 'RED' with the extension was burned from buyers seven seconds after purchase.

Scoping the 'airdrops fail' headline: after Arbitrum's airdrop, unique addresses stayed about 50% above pre-airdrop levels and TVL rose over 50% without a significant drop, but per-address transaction counts fell to under 75% of pre-airdrop. The authors call airdrops possibly necessary to attract users initially but insufficient to build a committed community.

Revoke does not undo an account-owner change. SetAuthority with the AccountOwner type (both token programs) gives the whole token account to a new owner and clears the delegate and allowance. The previous owner can then no longer sign for that account, so a victim cannot Revoke it. GoPlus says the new owner gains full control, which is more severe than a simple transfer. The SolPhishHunter authors say it is more direct and severe than Ethereum's approve-then-transfer pattern. Revoking approvals defends against Approve, not against SetAuthority or Assign.

Before the net-zero vote, the 2026 round was already smaller than the 2024 mandate. Jupiter's proposal describes the 'continue' option as a 200M JUP initial distribution after a checker release, a 200M JUP bonus pool and 300M JUP of Jupnet incentives (summing to the 700M the proposal says would be returned). BlockEden reports the DAO had cut the initial distribution from 700M to 200M to limit dilution.

GoPlus tested wallets in January 2024. Phantom and Backpack both showed an explicit warning for a SetAuthority transaction that changes a token account's owner, and users who chose 'Ignore and proceed anyway' still saw the balance change in the simulation. The post does not say whether the wallets warn on a delegate Approve.

Closing an empty associated token account is recoverable at the cost of fresh rent; burning is not. Streamflow says closed accounts cannot be restored but you can pay the rent again to recreate the associated token account, and Sol Incinerator lists a guide to reopening a closed account by re-depositing rent.

Published Solana drainer loss figures use different scopes and valuation bases, so they cannot be added or ranked. Scam Sniffer counted about $4.17M from about 3,947 victims for two drainers (Rainbow and Node) in roughly the month to 2024-01-13; Mandiant inferred at least $900k for CLINKSINK affiliates from the operator's roughly 20% share, valued 'at the time of analysis'; SolPhish totalled $1.10M at latest token prices; and Scam Sniffer's 2025 EVM series uses USD value at time of theft and calls itself a lower bound.

TokenTax says the One Big Beautiful Bill Act made the elimination of miscellaneous itemized deductions permanent after 2025, so a hobby-classified farmer cannot deduct gas, VPN or hardware costs against airdrop income; its example is $10,000 of income and $3,000 of costs, all taxed. Chief Counsel Advice 202302011 confirms only that section 67(g) suspended these deductions for 2018 through 2025. The permanence claim has one source; check the statute before relying on it.

Durable nonces also appear in a non-retail attack. CoinDesk reports that the 1 April 2026 Drift Protocol theft (at least $270 million; other outlets give up to $286 million) used durable-nonce transactions pre-signed by two members of a five-member Security Council who had been misled into approving. CoinDesk says no code bug was exploited and no private key was stolen. This was a multisig and governance compromise, not a wallet drainer. It shows the pre-signing risk at larger scale.

Supervised and ML sybil classifiers inherit the errors of their labels. Artemis (March 2024) pooled prior airdrop exclusion lists (Arbitrum, Hop) as sybil labels and published no accuracy or precision figures. The 2025 arXiv subgraph-LightGBM paper labelled addresses sybil if they were clustered and then either did not appeal or lost a manual appeal, and reports no label error rate, so a legitimate user who never appealed counts as sybil.

Tax tools bake in jurisdiction-specific defaults about airdrops, so a US filer cannot trust them unchecked. BittyTax (UK-focused) records its Airdrop type as not taxed as income because nothing is assumed done in return, and says to use Income when a service or condition applied; its README does not address spam. The article draws no cause and links the fall to weak performance of other Solana airdrops such as Wormhole W and Tensor TNSR.

Weiss Ratings (2024-01-30) argued that Solana airdrops had rallied right after launch (JTO rose 81% in two days to $4.40) while warning that the pattern only tracks the near term; JTO was already back near $1.30. In SolPhishHunter's dataset of labelled phishing accounts, 8,571 transactions were flagged as suspicious, about 3.26% of those accounts' transactions. Account authority transfers made up 2,272 (26.5%) of the flagged set. 2,171 of those were confirmed phishing, and 1,391 moved both wallet-account and token-account authority. The paper never mentions Approve or delegates. Its rules check only Transfer, Assign and SetAuthority, so it cannot show how common Approve phishing is.

A Token-2022 PermanentDelegate is a mint-level authority that can transfer or burn from any token account of the mint. Token account owners cannot revoke it. Revoke only clears the per-account delegate and delegated_amount fields, and CPI Guard still lets a permanent delegate act through CPI.

Scope for the 'airdrops fail' headline: two independent 2026 analyses of Hyperliquid's points-based HYPE airdrop (not Solana) agree that most recipients left but a small group stayed. Otomato (all 94,019 recipient wallets): 86% sold every token, 93.2% of the 271M HYPE left the receiving wallets, yet 29% of the largest allocations stayed active against 6.4% of the smallest, and 319 wallets (0.3%) did 92% of 30-day volume. Myshteri (about 2.0M addresses): D1/D7/D30 retention of 31/16/8% matches app benchmarks and D360 is 3%; 'Points buy activity; they evidently don't buy retention.'

Solana transaction fees are small and fixed. The base fee is 5,000 lamports (0.000005 SOL) per signature, with 50% burned and 50% paid to the block producer. The optional priority fee (compute unit price times compute unit limit, divided by 1,000,000 lamports) goes 100% to the validator since SIMD-0096 (status Activated). A transaction pays its fee whether it succeeds or fails.

A falling price does not create a deductible loss. Chief Counsel Advice 202302011 (released 2023-01-13, marked not to be used or cited as precedent) says a holder who still owns crypto that retains value, and has not sold, exchanged or abandoned it, has no section 165 loss, and that any such loss would be a miscellaneous itemized deduction suspended through 2025. Inferred effect: a farmer who reported an airdrop at a high receipt-date value cannot write it down until a sale, exchange or abandonment fixes the loss.

Cluster-size cutoffs are one way to limit over-blocking. ZKsync filtered 'all the clusters with more than 20 EOAs', which by construction leaves smaller clusters unfiltered. Arbitrum lists 'addresses transferring funds in a cluster of more than 20 addresses' as one example sybil pattern, alongside same-source funding and similar activity, and gives no threshold for 'similar activity'.

Treat vendor ROI statistics as unverified. A ChainScore Labs blog (an engineering consultancy) attributes to Nansen an analysis of 10 L2 airdrops with a median net profit of $47 and a mean of $1,850, and says over 80% of recipients sell within the first week in one place and 80% of tokens within 30 days in another, but a web search found no Nansen publication with those figures, and the page's case-study table cites no source. Its qualitative argument still works as a checklist: ROI that omits opportunity cost, bridge and swap gas, and the failure rate of the issuing protocol overstates return

Revoke cannot defend against an ownership transfer. The Revoke code checks the signature of the account's current owner (or, in Token-2022, its delegate). After SetAuthority moves the owner, the victim's signature no longer satisfies that check. This follows from the program source; no source tests recovery.

There is no specific IRS rule for spam or unsolicited worthless tokens. The practitioner view is that a token you cannot control or that has no supportable market value yields no taxable income, while a token with real value is ordinary income. The vendor guidance also warns against interacting with suspicious tokens, which links this concept to the spam-token safety siblings.

Token-2022's CPI Guard account extension, when its lock is enabled, makes Approve and SetAuthority fail when invoked through a cross-program invocation (errors CpiGuardApproveBlocked and CpiGuardSetAuthorityBlocked). It limits CPI-based approval grabs but does not stop a top-level Approve instruction the user signs.

In the Token-2022 code, SetAuthority with the PermanentDelegate type must be signed by the current permanent delegate. If no permanent delegate is set, the code returns AuthorityTypeNotSupported, so a cleared permanent delegate cannot be set again. The Solana docs say InitializePermanentDelegate must run before InitializeMint, so a mint cannot gain a permanent delegate after launch.

SetAuthority with AccountOwner on a token account changes the owner and also clears the delegate and delegated_amount. After the transfer the victim is no longer the owner, so the victim cannot sign Revoke for that account (inferred from validate_owner against account.owner). Revoking is a defence against Approve, not against ownership transfer.

Approve and Revoke both fail with AccountFrozen on a frozen token account, so a holder cannot revoke a delegate on a frozen account until the account is thawed, which only the mint's freeze authority can do.
