Secondary coverage can misstate a filter's rules. SolanaFloor says transactions under $5, short-term trading and circular trades 'were all grounds for disqualification'. Jupiter's own post says swaps under $5 only fail to count toward the Swap Score, while wallets were removed under three rules: trading for less than 3 weeks, a 50%+ failed-transaction rate, or exclusively circular trades. Check the issuer's post before relying on a news summary.

Solflare shows the warning 'Signing this transaction will allow your funds to be spent at a future date without your approval' when a transaction changes a token account's delegation. It lists revocation under Settings > Security & Privacy > Spending approvals. Solflare says it is one of few wallets that detect this.

Solflare shows the warning 'Signing this transaction will allow your funds to be spent at a future date without your approval' when a transaction changes a token account's delegation, and says it is one of the few wallets that detect this. Revoking in Solflare is under Settings, Security and Privacy, Spending approvals.

Linea is the only issuer I found that published a count of filter errors reversed on appeal. Linea's X post of 2025-02-17, relayed by Bitget News on 2025-02-18, says it 'completed the review of sybil appeals' and 'identified 3.5k false positives which have been removed from the sybil list'. Against about 516,960 flagged addresses that is about 0.7% (my arithmetic). Linea did not publish how many appeals it received. So 0.7% is a floor on the error rate among flagged wallets: it counts only errors that someone appealed and Linea accepted. It is not a measured false-positive rate.

Receipt turns on control, not on the ledger entry alone. Rev. Rul. 2019-24 says a holder has not received an airdrop if they cannot exercise dominion and control, for example when an exchange-managed wallet does not yet support the new coin. The holder is treated as receiving it later, when they can transfer, sell, exchange or otherwise dispose of it. IRS FAQ 105 repeats that test, and a TaxAudit worked example values units on the later control date (2024-03-18), not the earlier deposit date (2024-03-12).

Vendors say losses from an airdrop scam usually cannot be deducted. TaxAudit says personal theft losses, meaning losses not connected with a trade or business, a for-profit investment or a federally declared disaster, were generally nondeductible for 2018 through 2025 under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act and may stay so if that act is extended. CoinLedger says such casualty losses typically can't be deducted. Their status after 2025 was not checked against a primary source.

Automation and fee timing cut a farmer's labour and fee cost. A farming dashboard described by Kerman Kohli (2023) lets users set bridge routes, random action probabilities, sleep intervals, automatic expense tracking and automatic withdrawal to an exchange. A research team told The Block it had started trialling software that randomises amounts and frequency, while describing its manual work as slow. TierDrop notes that farmers lower costs by sending transactions when fees are low, by automating free tasks and by using cheap labour. None of these sources publishes tool prices.

Revoking cannot help once a key or recovery phrase is stolen, because the attacker signs as the owner and can sign any instruction. In the 2 August 2022 Slope wallet incident, about 9,200 to 9,300 wallets were drained (sources give 9,229, 9,231 and 9,321) with transactions signed by valid private keys. Sentry and Ackee both say the transactions were correctly signed. MadeOnSol advises moving to a new wallet if a key may be exposed.

Trusta's published sybil method has two phases: community detection (Louvain, K-Core) on asset-transfer graphs, then a K-means-style refinement on behavioural similarity 'to reduce false positives from Phase 1'. Trusta rejects anomaly detection because 'they behave similarly to regular users', publishes no precision or recall, and its Gitcoin hackathon repository reports 16,994 'High Risk Sybils' without thresholds or validation. An independent group describes the approach as needing per-airdrop analysis and substantial human effort to set clustering parameters.

Streamflow's Sybil Checker documentation (9 September 2025) describes a paid tool: 0.09 USDC per wallet, 10 to 100,000 addresses per run. It maps links between wallets through transfers, shared funders or exchanges, flags wallets once the number linked to one entity exceeds a configurable threshold, offers timeframe and transfer-limit settings, and returns a report listing each flagged wallet's detection method. The page describes no false-positive handling, appeals or manual-review advice.

Delegation has legitimate uses, so a delegate is a risk signal and not proof of an attack. Solana's Spend Permissions page lists payment processors, automated payroll, escrow, trading platforms and card issuance. A dApp developer also reports using an SPL delegate approval to a settlement program. Check who the delegate is and how large the allowance is before revoking or signing.

Account authority transfer (AAT) drains change who controls an account instead of moving tokens. The Assign instruction sets a wallet account's owner to an attacker's program. SetAuthority sets the attacker as owner of a token account. The docs.rs entry for Assign lists the assigned account as a required signer, so the victim must sign. Afterwards the funds still show in the wallet, but the victim cannot move or revoke them. SolPhishHunter found 2,171 such phishing transactions. SlowMist documented a December 2025 victim who lost more than $3 million.

Raydium's trust-and-safety page says closing airdropped accounts to reclaim about 0.002 SOL is safe under the standard SPL Token program, but that Token-2022 tokens with transfer hooks 'can execute arbitrary code on close', so it advises leaving them. In the solana-program/token-2022 main branch (commit c8a15ff9, read 2026-11-06) the only call into a transfer-hook program is the Execute CPI at the end of process_transfer. process_burn and process_close_account contain no transfer-hook reference, and the Token-2022 docs describe the hook as called during a transfer. Most Solana phishing signatures request direct transfers rather than the token approvals typical of Ethereum thefts, and Solana lets one transaction carry many instructions, so a single signature can drain SOL and several token types at once. The SolPhish paper calls this pattern STMT (single transaction, multiple transfers).

ScamSniffer reported that most Solana phishing signatures start direct transfers, unlike the approval-based thefts common on Ethereum. SolPhishHunter's three Solana-specific transaction types agree: single transaction with multiple transfers (STMT), account authority transfer (AAT) and impersonation of system accounts (ISA). None of the three is an allowance approval. Caveat: SolPhishHunter scoped itself to Solana-specific types by design, so it cannot show that approvals are rare.

Jupiter drafted its Jupuary criteria in public community forum threads with competing proposals: count JUP/JLP/JUPSOL held in Meteora or Kamino as holdings, treat staking and holding as multipliers rather than base criteria, down-weight plain swaps as saturated, and favour DCA, limit orders and perps. The fetched threads show no official team reply and no numeric weights. Critics also warned that tracking every participant's activity across platforms invites disputes.

Token-2022 mints can stop a holder from burning their own tokens. With the Permissioned Burn extension the standard Burn and BurnChecked instructions are rejected and each burn needs the mint's burn authority as an extra signer. With the Pausable extension a paused mint aborts burns as well as transfers. With CPI Guard enabled, a burn made through a CPI must be signed by a delegate rather than the owner. A spam token that cannot be burned can be emptied only by transferring it away, which the sources advise against, so the practical choice is to hide it. Both extensions appear in the Token-202

An empty account is not always safe to close. Jupiter warns that closing your associated token account during an active DCA order leaves the purchased tokens in the vault instead of your wallet. Sol Incinerator says an empty account may be waiting for a bot's next trade. MadeOnSol says not to close the account of a token you actively use in lending, staking or LP even when the balance shows 0. Streamflow warns that its value slider can select accounts that still hold tokens, and that closing them permanently destroys their contents. Review the selection before approving.

Jupiter held 200M of the 700M JUP back as 'Carrots' to be paid out across 2025 instead of in January. Uses named in the post: bonuses for recipients who claim and stake through Jupiter Mobile, appeals, 'Good Cats' contributors, and growth programs. SolanaFloor describes the Carrot system as a way to cut sell pressure by rewarding recipients who stake.

Jupiter held back 200M of the 700M JUP as 'Carrots', paid over the year instead of in January. The stated uses: incentives to claim and stake through Jupiter Mobile, paying appeals (a 3-month window), 'Good Cats' contributors, and later growth programs. SolanaFloor reported 500M JUP immediately claimable and 200M reserved for Good Cat and Carrot allocations, and described Carrots as a way to cut immediate dumping by rewarding recipients who stake.

Jupiter's first Jupuary proposal (700M JUP for each of two Januaries, about $1.7B) got 58% support against a 70% threshold and failed; a revised plan passed with over 87%. The founder said JUP should go to people who can become long-term members rather than farmers or a small group of heavy users. The January 2024 drop had distributed 1.35B JUP (13.5% of supply) to nearly 1M wallets.

Closing moves every lamport in the token account to the destination account named in the instruction. The signer must be the account's close authority if one is set, otherwise its owner. So the holder, not the sender who funded the account, chooses where the rent goes. If CPI Guard is enabled and the close runs inside a cross-program call, the destination must be the account owner. Sol Incinerator adds that a separate close authority, if there is one, must approve instead of the owner.

SolPhishHunter reports 93.96% overall precision, but it tests on 169 labeled phishing accounts (262,719 transactions) against a negative set of the 200 highest-value Solscan accounts (274,705 transactions), where it raised 5 false positives (all AAT). That negative set is clean by design, so false-positive rates on ordinary wallets are untested. The paper's own figures also differ internally (precision 93.96% vs 94.01%; total loss 'nearly $1.07 million' in text vs $1,099,815.98 in its tables).

A Solana signature commits to the exact message bytes (fee payer, blockhash or nonce, every account with its signer and writable flags, and instruction data), not to what a called program will do later. Hold-and-flip drainers exploit that gap: Blowfish described Aqua and Vanish drainers that keep the signed transaction and flip a conditional in the dApp's on-chain program through a separate transaction, so a transaction that appeared to send SOL to the user takes it instead. Blockaid traced a Vanish case where the state-setting transaction landed seven blocks before the drain (block 247363970

Filtering is usually one layer among several, and the other layers lower the cost of filter errors. ZKsync says eligibility rules, value scaling and multipliers removed most bot swarms before its sybil step. Streamflow, a Solana token-distribution vendor that sells vesting and a sybil checker, argues vested distribution 'complements, rather than replaces' filtering and shrinks the payoff of sybils that slip through; it recommends a pre-announcement snapshot and a 60 to 90 day minimum wallet age and does not discuss wrongly excluded users. The common bait pattern: a scammer airdrops a worthless token or NFT whose name, symbol or external-link field holds a phishing 'claim' URL. In the Rainbow Drainer campaign the URL sat in the Name and External Link of NFTs sent to ZERO token holders, and the operators later edited the name and link of an already-deployed NFT address to launch a different lure (MEMEDROP) instead of minting new ones.

Lighthouse Protocol adds assertion instructions that fail the transaction if the final state differs from what the simulation showed. Phantom says it worked with Lighthouse on 'Guard instructions' for this purpose. Blockaid notes limits: extra instructions can push a transaction over Solana's size limit, and assertions do not stop most drains, which need no simulation bypass. Blockaid recommends layering program-code analysis, address reputation checks and dApp scanning.

Approval abuse is not the main drain method on Solana. ScamSniffer (January 2024) says the majority of Solana phishing signatures start direct transfers, unlike Ethereum, where malicious approvals dominate. GoPlus's worked examples are direct SOL and multi-token transfers. In SolPhishHunter's flagged set, 32% are single transactions with multiple transfers. None of the three gives a share for Approve.

In the SolPhish dataset AAT transactions were the rarest type by count among the three but caused about $812k of roughly $1.10M detected losses (about 74%); the paper's own totals are internally inconsistent in places (e.g. 8,571 vs 8,576 transactions; 39 vs 64 phishing accounts).

The SolPhish study detected 8,058 Solana-specific phishing transactions worth about $1.10M ($1,099,815.98). Account Authority Transfer was the fewest by count (2,171, against 2,438 multi-transfer and 3,449 impersonation transactions) but carried $812,219.75, or 73.85%, of the loss. The paper values an AAT loss as the total value of tokens in accounts whose authority moved, at latest prices from Oklink, so that share is an exposure estimate rather than confirmed outflow.

Hiding is the non-destructive first step; burning is permanent and closing an empty account is the non-destructive cleanup. Data Clinic advises hiding rather than deleting, and Sol Incinerator states burning is permanent while closing an empty account does not burn assets held in other accounts.

Because anybody can create an associated token account for any wallet, a sender can re-create an account the holder closed and send the token again. This is an inference from the ATA rule; no source measures whether spam returns after a cleanup, so treat cleanup as optional maintenance rather than a fix.

Cleanup tools can destroy value if the selection is wrong, so judge by token count, not dollar value. Sol Incinerator says a token worth less than a cent can still have a balance and to check the number of tokens rather than the dollar value. Streamflow's Dust Collector treats accounts under $0.001 as candidates and warns that its value slider 'lets you close token accounts regardless of their balance', which permanently destroys the tokens in any account that still holds funds. Jumpbit's author likewise lists 'Never Close Accounts with Balances' and 'Test with Small Batch First'.

The rent a closed account returns is changing. The minimum balance is (128 + data_len) x lamports_per_byte, and SIMD-0437 cuts lamports_per_byte from 6,960 to 696 in five feature-gated steps. Step 1 (6,333) went live on mainnet on 2026-09-03 and step 2 (5,080) at epoch 1033 on 2026-09-11, so a new 165-byte token account now needs 1,488,440 lamports (about 0.00148844 SOL) instead of 2,039,280 (about 0.00203928 SOL). Steps 3 to 5 (2,575, 1,322 and 696 lamports per byte) had not activated as of 2026-10-28; Anza's schedule targeted 2026-11-09 for the start of Agave 4.4 feature activation, subject

Entry-cost estimates for a Solana farmer are capital-sized rather than fee-sized, and they come from promotional sources. Yellow.com research (2026-03-24), citing a Zipmex estimate, says farmers can start with $50 to $100 in SOL and that meaningful multi-protocol activity takes $300 to $500. HFA Research (2024-02-01), whose author discloses he farms Solana and Celestia, claims people turned $50 into $10,000 by staking SOL with Jito. Neither source prices time, tooling or the chance of no payout.

Do not interact with an unsolicited token only to dispose of it for tax purposes. TokenTax advises seeking tax advice for a material amount rather than interacting with an unknown smart contract to effect a disposal. KoinX says never to click token links, swap, transfer or connect a wallet to claim an unknown token, and to hide or mark it as spam instead. Koinly warns that any action involving a worthless spam token may lead to a loss of funds.

Some launches now use points as priority access to a token sale instead of a free airdrop. Infinex 'Patron Sales' require points to qualify for its ICO (Ignas, October 2024). In January 2026 Ranger, a MetaDAO ICO on Solana selling 39% of supply, guaranteed point holders a dedicated allocation bucket with unfilled allocation rolling to public buyers; the analysis behind this says it rewards early users without giving away 10% to 30% of supply, and notes MetaDAO's last six ICOs were oversubscribed so buyers got about 5% of desired exposure.

Detection zeroes the reward rather than trimming it, so expected value per wallet falls as wallets become linked. Hop built its final distribution after removing reported sybil groups, and the reported hunters received nothing. Farmers told The Block that projects look for clusters of connected wallets and eliminate them; one keeps wallets unlinked and targets larger projects because smaller ones hunt farmers harder. CoinMarketCap notes that points programmes can invalidate points from addresses that farm with multiple accounts. Farmers respond with fewer wallets, manual activity or randomised

Jupiter also used a Swap Score as a soft filter that down-weights instead of excluding. Only swaps over $5 count. SOL-to-SOL swaps such as jupSOL to SOL are discounted heavily, and stablecoin-to-stablecoin swaps are discounted very heavily. All other trades count at 100% of nominal volume. The team says it kept discounted swaps in the score because many organic traders make them. Allocations are per wallet and in tiers. SolanaFloor confirms that swaps under $5, circular trades and illiquid-token swaps do not add to the score.

Large-scale farming raises a hobby-versus-business question that casual recipients do not face. IRS fact sheet FS-2022-38 lists profit-motive factors (business-like records, expertise, time and effort, profit expectation and history, losses beyond the taxpayer's control, personal pleasure) and says hobby income goes on Schedule 1, line 8, with no loss offset against other income. TokenTax applies the section 183 factor test to farmers: business status means Schedule C and 15.3% self-employment tax, hobby status means Schedule 1 line 8j. Lighthouse adds an assertion instruction that fails the transaction if the final state differs from the simulated state, which counters TOCTOU drainers; Blockaid notes it can push transactions past Solana's size limit, does not address most wallet-draining attempts, and recommends layered defences (program analysis, address reputation, dApp scanning).

Return figures in this literature differ on four axes that change the answer. Sample: X-explore's hunters are defined by having received tokens in several airdrops, so they are selected on success. Expected versus realised: the Hop profits are modelled for addresses that were disqualified and paid nothing. Price basis: the HYPE median seller exited at $6.25 while the token stood at $67, so a claim-day price and a later price give different answers. Cost basis: Hop counts gas and bridge fees only, and The Block's farmer figures leave out capital, time and failed attempts.

A Chaos Labs author's thread (unrolled 2024-07-15) quotes an earlier post saying the LayerZero sybil list 'now features ~440K addresses' after the team reviewed 'all appeals and Sybil Bounty reports', down from over 800K in the first scan. The same page reports an interim EVM-only analysis of 4.82M users with about 14.5% classified as sybil. I found no second source for the ~440K figure, and it may describe the Chaos Labs list rather than LayerZero's combined list. Treat it as unconfirmed.

Wormhole builds an 'ownership graph' that gives one user ID to a cluster of wallets and spreads the cluster's reward across all of its wallets, so a person with several wallets counts as one user instead of being excluded. The minimum cumulative transfer value (median about $1,500 after adjustments) is tested across all linked wallets. A side effect that Wormhole's FAQ admits is that wallets with a single small transaction can qualify, which may confuse users.

Treating a promotional airdrop as a gift is not supported by any authority found. IRS FAQ 75 excuses income only for a bona fide gift. An Intuit community answer (2022-02-03) calls airdrops marketing incentives rather than gifts, taxable 'regardless of whether you intended to own these coins'. No source found applies the section 102 gift test to an airdrop.

Revoking does not fix a compromised key or seed phrase. In the August 2022 Slope incident, drains began at 22:37 UTC on 2 August 2022, and analysis showed private keys were used to sign the transactions, so the wallets had to be abandoned rather than cleaned up. Phantom-style guidance likewise says to move assets to a new recovery phrase if a key may be exposed.

Across three Jupuary drops, Jupiter narrowed eligibility from every wallet to qualified users and stakers. The January 2024 round paid all ~955,000 wallets that had used Jupiter before the 2 November 2023 cutoff, 'bot or not', with a flat 200 JUP each. The January 2025 round added volume thresholds, sybil removal and per-transaction scoring, and paid about 2 million of 10 million-plus wallets. The planned 2026 round limited the initial airdrop to stakers and users who had paid fees, with a 30 January 2026 snapshot.

Lookalike cleanup sites exist. PCrisk documents sol-incinerator[.]tax (updated 2026-01-14), a copy of sol-incinerator.com that promises rewards for burning tokens, is spread through fake social accounts and ads, and runs a wallet drainer once a wallet connects. Guidance from the real tool and others: approve each transaction in your own wallet, check that the simulation shows a positive SOL change for the accounts you selected, bookmark the official domain, ignore links from Discord, Telegram or tweets claiming to be these tools, and never enter a recovery phrase or private key into a cleanup

Fake cleanup sites target people trying to remove spam. PCrisk (updated 2026-01-14) documents sol-incinerator[.]tax, a fraudulent copy of sol-incinerator.com that promises rewards for burning tokens and activates a crypto drainer once a wallet is connected. The real tool says to approve each transaction in your own wallet and never to enter a recovery phrase or private key into a cleanup site. Raydium describes the same pattern more broadly: look-alike sites promoted with ads for brand terms that harvest signatures, with bookmarking the real domain as the defense.

Eligibility metrics that are cheap to hit get farmed. Remedies in the literature: scale rewards to costs users actually bear (low fees make transaction-count thresholds cheap), weight by time and amount, require multi-step activity, cap per-user rewards, change criteria across multiple rounds, and reward long-term users. Drift's loyalty weighting filtered newer sybil farmers; zkLend's unvetted airdrop attracted speculators.

Receiving a spam token or NFT does not by itself give anyone control of a wallet. Solflare says the mere presence of an NFT or token is not an inherent threat; the loss comes from opening its links or connecting to its site. The exceptions are mint-level powers such as a permanent delegate or freeze authority, which act only on balances of that one mint. Phantom still advises treating every unsolicited token as a scam and never approving anything tied to it.

The Token-2022 permanent-delegate extension gives a designated authority unlimited delegate privileges over every token account of that mint: it can burn or transfer tokens from any holder and can bypass CPI Guard. In September 2024 a holder of a token called RED had their balance burned about seven seconds after a swap. Jupiter and RugCheck then added indicators that flag mints with the extension. Check a mint's extensions before treating any held balance as yours.

Closing authority and account ownership matter: the account owner, or its separate close authority, must approve a close. With CPI Guard enabled on a Token-2022 account, the lamport destination of a close must be the account owner. Using the spl-token CLI requires signing with the wallet secret key unless a Ledger is used.

The Token-2022 permanent-delegate extension gives a designated authority unlimited delegate privileges over every token account of the mint, so it can burn or transfer any holder's tokens and bypass CPI Guard. In September 2024 a buyer of a token called RED had the whole purchase burned about seven seconds after the swap; Jupiter and RugCheck then added indicators for mints with the extension. Check a mint's extensions before treating a held balance as yours.

Solana points programs write anti-gaming rules into the criteria: Tensor Season 1 required at least 500 SOL of NFT trading volume and banned wash trading; Tensor Season 2 rewarded loyalty (not listing on other marketplaces); Parcl can revoke points from self-referrals; Kamino limits LST-only or stablecoin-only farming. Points can also distort behaviour: Zeta users felt pushed into market orders and took slippage.

Signals the sources give for recognizing a spam token: you did not acquire it and do not recognize it (Phantom: an unrecognized asset is 'usually spam'). Its name, ticker, logo and metadata are chosen by the creator, so the mint address is the token's real identity (Raydium), and Jupiter does not verify metadata unless the token passed its verification. In Data Clinic's BLOSK example a block-explorer lookup, done without connecting a wallet, showed a brand-new, low-liquidity token with almost no real trading. Jupiter Shield flags Not Verified, Low Organic Activity, New Listing, Has Freeze Auth

Self-reported farmer returns are large per account but selective, unaudited and priced at claim. The Block (2023-04-06): one farmer paid about $1,000 in fees across 1,000+ transactions and about $300,000 of volume for an Arbitrum airdrop of about $15,000; another used 100 wallets on Arbitrum (the article infers at least 62,500 ARB, about $80,000 at launch); one team claimed close to $1 million, though its itemised amounts (Blur about $300K, Arbitrum about $180K, Aptos $125K, Optimism $120K) sum to $725K. Interviewees in Odaily (via WuBlockchain, 2025-02-25) report about $1,000 per account on 5

Signals the guidance gives for recognizing a spam token: it arrived unsolicited; its name or metadata carries a URL or a claim prompt (Raydium's example 'Visit xyz-airdrop.com to claim!'); a Solscan check, made without connecting a wallet, shows a brand-new, low-liquidity token with almost no real trading (Data Clinic); identity is the mint address, since tickers and logos can be set by anyone (Raydium); and creator-retained freeze or mint authority, creator-only liquidity, or absence from CoinGecko and CoinMarketCap are red flags (Cielo). A clean scanner result is not proof of legitimacy.

The 60M JUP staker pool in Jupuary 2025 paid on time-weighted stake, not on a single snapshot, so staking, unstaking and wallet moves during the year did not distort the result. Two stackable bonuses rewarded behaviour: 'Super Voters' (voted on 13 or more proposals) and 'Super Stakers' (never unstaked). The stacked maximum was about 0.313 JUP per time-weighted JUP staked.

Unclaimed airdrop tokens were recycled into staker rewards. A community proposal in October 2024 noted that 215M unclaimed JUP from round 1 had been allocated to JUP stakers, and Jupiter's February 2026 proposal says Active Staking Rewards (ASR), 50M JUP per quarter, are paid from circulating tokens from previously unclaimed Jupuary, so they add no new emissions.

Solana issuers publish an eligibility checker before the claim opens. Jupiter's checker went live on 15 January 2025 and the claim followed about a week later; Drift's was on drift.foundation; Jito used its jito.network/airdrop page. For Jupuary 2026, Jupiter planned to release the checker only about a week after the governance vote even though the snapshot had been taken on 30 January 2026, and commenters asked for the checker first.

Besides bundled transfers, a malicious Solana transaction can hide in a token Approve (delegate with an allowance), a signed off-chain message, or an account-authority change. The SolPhish paper defines Account Authority Transfer (AAT) as a System Program Assign (changes the wallet's owner program) or a SetAuthority of type 'account owner', and notes Ethereum-style payload detection does not transfer directly.

Public detail on Jito's sybil filter is thin. A Decentralised.co article says the Jito Foundation 'used sybil detection techniques to weed out airdrop farmers', ranked eligible addresses by points (stake size, duration, DeFi activity) into ten tiers, and dropped 80 million tokens across 9,852 addresses in the staker and user pool. It describes no technique, no exclusion count and no appeal route, and says detection 'will always be more probabilistic than deterministic'.

Wallet and DEX guidance converges on the same default for airdropped tokens: treat them as likely spam, do not follow links or instructions attached to them, do not click them or visit their websites, do not try to sell them, and hide them (report as spam in Phantom; turn on hide-unknown-tokens in other wallets). Receiving an unfamiliar token does not mean the wallet is compromised.

The payoff for cleaning up one spam account is small and shrinking. The Solana Foundation figure quoted by Solana Compass puts a standard token account's rent at about $0.159 before SIMD-0437 and about $0.016 after all five steps; in SOL that is 0.00204 for accounts created before the cuts, 0.00149 for new ones now, and 0.0002 at step 5. The case for burn-and-close is therefore bulk rent recovery for wallets holding hundreds of accounts, not safety: none of the guidance reviewed says that merely holding an unsolicited token is harmful, and Raydium's advice for airdropped accounts is to leave t

Spam-token detection signals documented for EVM chains by Forta include phishing metadata links, token name/symbol copied from an existing token, mass airdrop with little post-airdrop activity, and one creator deploying many tokens quickly; Forta states the majority of spam tokens are phishing tokens. This is an EVM source and 2023 data, and no equivalent Solana-specific study was found.

SolPhishHunter classifies a transaction by instruction pattern after excluding market activity: multi-transfer drains need more than two Transfer instructions and at least two token balances going from non-zero to zero; AAT needs an Assign instruction or a SetAuthority of type 'account owner'; impersonation needs a balance-depleting transfer to an address that starts with 'Compu' or ends in a run of '1'.
